progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b06: barriers; histamine from damaged cells and mast cells widens small vessels and makes them leaky (redness, warmth, swelling); neutrophils follow a chemical trail and engulf bacteria; dendritic cells carry pieces of the pathogen to a lymph node; "Block, alarm, eat, alert"; the response strip's four rungs. From b07: antigen; each B cell has one receptor shape, made before infection; clonal selection; a helper T cell's go-ahead; clonal expansion; plasma cells release antibodies; memory B cells; antibodies block, clump and coat; the strip's five B cell chips ("fit", "go-ahead", "clone", "plasma cells", "antibodies bind"). From b08: helper T cells are switched on by pieces shown on dendritic cells and give B cells the go-ahead. From b09: primary and secondary responses; the antibody graph and log scale; memory stored mainly in cells; vaccination and boosters; active and passive, natural and artificial, and the two questions ("Who made the antibodies?"; "naturally, or by medical treatment?"). Not assumed: lyssavirus (glossed in the Q3 stem as "a close relative of rabies"), immunoglobulin (screen only; spoken as "rabies antibodies").
progression.startsWith: An unfamiliar immunity question: a list of events, an antibody graph, or a case. The video opens: Immunity questions often ask you to do one of three things.
progression.stopsAfter: ordering eight events from a pathogen's entry through the innate response (barrier, histamine and leaky vessels, neutrophils, dendritic cell to lymph node) to the adaptive response (B cells that fit bind the antigen, helper T cell go-ahead, clone of plasma and memory cells, antibodies bind) and explaining why antibody takes about a week (few fitting B cells must meet the antigen, get the go-ahead and divide many times; innate defences hold the bacteria meanwhile); reading a log-scale antibody graph (lag, peak values, a protective level) and comparing two doses with data (about fifty times higher, sooner, above the protective line), then explaining the difference by memory cells from the first dose; classifying a rabies antibody injection as artificial passive and a rabies vaccine as artificial active immunity, and explaining why both are given (immediate cover while the slower active response builds lasting protection, possible because symptoms take weeks or months).
progression.nextLesson: how hygiene and quarantine interrupt spread (route entry bio-m7-b10).

teaching.task: When an immunity question asks you to put the response in order, read an antibody graph, or name someone's immunity, how do you work it out step by step?
teaching.causalExplanation: Why histamine causes redness and swelling (2b, one clause, recalled); why the dendritic cell links the two halves (2b, 2c); why antibody takes about a week (few fitting cells, selection, go-ahead and many divisions; 2d); why the second dose gives a faster, much higher response (memory cells from the first dose, fewer divisions, quick change to plasma cells; 3c); why the injected antibodies act at once but fade (ready-made, no B cells selected; 4c); why the vaccine needs time (a primary response; 4c, 4d); why giving both works (immediate cover while memory builds, and a long incubation; 4c).
teaching.conversationalApproach: Immunity questions ask you to put the response in order, read an antibody graph or name someone's immunity, and each walkthrough works from the question one step at a time. Q1 orders eight events after soil bacteria enter a gardener's cut: the barrier first, then the innate alarm, phagocytes and dendritic cell, then selection of the few fitting B cells, the helper T cell's go-ahead, division into a clone and plasma cells releasing antibodies, and part b explains why that takes about a week; Q2 reads a two-dose vaccine graph on a log scale, checking that each gridline is ten times the one below before comparing the lag and the peaks, then explains the primary and secondary responses from memory cells; Q3 classifies the antibody injection and the vaccine given after a flying fox scratch as passive and active by asking who made the antibodies, and explains why both are given (the injection covers the gap while the vaccine builds memory). Each question ends with its spoken, crossed classic mistake (the body designs an antibody, counting gridlines as a linear scale, the vaccine works straight away), and the decision board gives the first move for each kind of question.
teaching.openingDecision: Immunity questions often ask you to do one of three things. Put the response in order, from the moment a pathogen gets in to the moment antibodies appear. Read a graph of antibody levels. Or name the immunity someone has, active or passive, natural or artificial. Each one hides a trap that costs marks. Here are three HSC-style questions, one of each. Pause and try each one, then we'll work through it together.
teaching.understandingCheck: Three, each 10 s with the countdown and every demand and condition visible (2a, 3a, 4a). Nothing answer-bearing during the holds.
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (2017, `docs/production/programme/syllabus/bio-2017-y12.json`; practice and transfer only, first coverage stays with b06 to b09): B7-IQ2-02 (p 54): "analyse responses to the presence of pathogens by assessing the physical and chemical changes that occur in the host animals cells and tissues (ACSBL119, ACSBL120, ACSBL121, ACSBL122)". Q1 event E and scene 2b (histamine, a chemical change, causing vessel widening and leaking, physical changes). B7-IQ3-01 (p 54): "investigate and model the innate and adaptive immune systems in the human body (ACSBL119)". Q1 (sequence the whole model, b06 to b08's response strip). B7-IQ3-02 (p 54): "explain how the immune system responds after primary exposure to a pathogen, including innate and acquired immunity". Q1 part (b) and Q2. B7-IQ4-02 (p 55): "investigate procedures that can be employed to prevent the spread of disease, including but not limited to: (ACSBL124)", with the listed item "vaccination, including passive and active immunity (ACSBL100, ACSBL123)". Q2 (a two-dose vaccine) and Q3 (post-exposure antibodies and vaccine).

design.visualSystem: One practice board throughout, in m6-g01's layout: top-left the question card (stem, data and demands as an exam prints them, with the "HSC-style question, written for HSCScience" tag), kept readable through the whole question; the working fills the right two thirds; a type badge top-right ("Sequence", "Antibody graph", "Type of immunity"), hidden during each attempt. When the walkthrough starts, the card shrinks to a strip and each given is underlined in amber in the question text at the cue where it is used (no givens card). Earlier questions are cleared before the next card writes on. Q1's working is b06 to b08's response strip, rebuilt rung by rung as each event card slides onto its rung, with small cell thumbnails (existing plates). Q2's working is the coded `lineGraph` (log axis, protective line, two exposure arrows) with reading guides. Q3's working is b09's coded two-by-two immunity table plus a small coded two-curve sketch (injected antibodies, own antibodies). No people, hands or faces: the gardener and the wildlife carer are words only; the cut appears only as the secateurs plate and a bacterium plate; the flying fox is an animal plate alone. Coded elements are abstract only. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): besides the question strip, at most about three bright text items in the working area at once; each working tag fades when the next cue lands. Plates are scaled proportionally, never stretched.
design.transitionPlan: The heading writes on and three small stimulus thumbnails fan out, one per cue (the ResponseStrip, an antibody graph and the ImmunityTable); each question opens on a fresh board with the type badge hidden while the worded card writes with the secateurs and wound, vaccine vial or flying fox plate small at its corner; the walkthrough shrinks the card to a strip, lights the type badge and underlines each given in amber as it is used; event letters slide into the ResponseStrip's innate rungs and then b07's five adaptive chip slots, and a short day axis draws for part b; the graph enlarges as the log axis gridlines light, the lag brackets and the peak readings write, and b09's cell field fills for memory cells; b09's ImmunityTable fills its passive and active cells and a two-curve sketch shows the gap being covered; each classic mistake writes as a chip and takes a grey scribble cross; the check strip returns full size as the two-column decision board, row by row; scene crossfade with settle.
